speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Payette.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: You're not? Where are you from?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I have a sister in Waukesha, Wisconsin. That's not too far from Michigan.

words: And then I spent some time in Virginia and then I came out here.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: So you are one of these, what do I call it? What are you connected with? Government project, isn't it?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Yes.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I lived in Troy before I came here and I had relatives and friends in Moscow, and I used to go back and forth to Moscow. I worked at the infirmary at the University. I'm real interested in [unintelligible] so I graduated from nursing school.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Where were you living before you came there?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Reinbeck, Iowa.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: What year did you arrive in Idaho?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: It must have been 1900.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: And how did you come?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: By train. Five families going in the Pullman coach. These five families and there were 19 youngsters in this one Pullman coach, and if you don't thing the Pullman porter had some fun keeping them quiet and keeping them in order!

speaker: Connie Richards
words: I bet! So, who were the companions on the trip? Did you have your mother and father? Marie Flodberg 4

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Yes. Two sisters; there were three girls at that time.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: No brothers?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: My brother was born here.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: And there were four other families?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Yes, they all came from Iowa, that same area in Iowa. There must have been more relatives.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: If you can talk to me a little bit about your mother's family, what was her maiden name?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Klingebiehl, and her name was Elizabeth.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: And when was she born, do you know?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: 1866, in June.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: And where was she born?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: In Germany.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Do you know what part? Marie Flodberg 5

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: The western part of Germany near the French border.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: And you tell me that I have a fancy name? [Laughter.]

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Is it French?

speaker: Connie Richards
words: It's a Luxembourg.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, that's in Germany, a portion of Germany. That's in the eastern part of Germany.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: I think so. When did your mother die, what year?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: 1923, I think.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Do you know what year she got married?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: In 1893, at the beginning of the year, and I came along at the end of the year. Like a lot of youngsters. She was married on Valentine's Day.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Was your mother always a homemaker?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, she came to this country with her mother. Her brother lived in Illinois and she and her mother came to Illinois. She worked as a maid in a home in a wealthy family. That's where she was until she came to visit her sister in Iowa and met my Marie Flodberg 6 dad and stayed.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Did they homestead, or what did your parents do?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: No, he bought the farm for $90. That was his deposit on it. She was a farmer's wife.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Can you remember some of the things she used to do on the farm?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, I don't think she did any more than did housework, what you would call, baking, cooking, canning and things of that sort. She didn't work in the fields like some women did.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: So she didn't milk the cow or anything like that?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I don't think she did, not that I know of. We had a dairy and she and Dad did the milking together.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: What was your father's name?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: John Peters.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: And do you know his date of birth?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: March of 1857. Marie Flodberg 7

speaker: Connie Richards
words: And where was he born?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Tunning, Germany. That was right near the Danish border.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: They both came from Germany and they met over in Iowa. And the date of his death?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: July of 1934, I guess it was.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Can you remember his occupation; what did he do when he came here?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: He was a farmer when he came here.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: He hadn't done anything in Germany then?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: No, he was in the service and he took French leave, I guess, when he came to this country. Like so many boys did at that time. They were sentenced to the army and then when they had a good chance -- he was on vacation or on leave, you call it, and he and someone else came to this country. He had a brother in Illinois and I guess he came to Illinois and then migrated to Iowa. I don't know too much of those details, but I do know that he had a brother in Illinois and then migrated to Iowa. You know, sometimes they don't tell you those things if you ask. A lot of times your mother is more confidential to you than your dad is. Marie Flodberg 8 And my mother left a sister in Germany, and her name was, hmmm, now the name slips me. What's this aviator that landed in Germany and is now serving time in Germany. I have a peculiar feeling that he might be my cousin because my mother's sister was married to a man by that name. The last couple days the name, it slipped my mind. I guess I am getting old.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: So, your father was first in the service and then he was a farmer and all the rest of his life?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, until we came to Idaho he did various things. When we came to Idaho we had a peach orchard and [unintelligible]. He bought some real estate and took care of that and farmed it. The town of Fruitland here in Idaho, was an 80 acre fruit orchard that he had and owned and it finally was blossomed out into a town and so I guess that's where they got the name of Fruitland because of the 80 acre prune orchard.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Would you tell me the names of your sisters?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Elizabeth, Anna and Emma.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: And you didn't have a brother?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: My brother died when he was five years old.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: What was his name? Marie Flodberg 9

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Rudolph.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: How did he die?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Oh, polio, I think. I was only ten years old at the time, so that's all I remember about that.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Can you remember, I'm sure it was awful upsetting to your mother.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: That was the thing. After he passed away, then they decided to go back to Iowa. He died here in Idaho and they just felt they did the wrong thing by coming down here -- he was born here.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Can you remember at that time, how they handled the funeral services? Was he buried at your home?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: The body was in the home. We had one of those old couches, if you remember, where they come up so that the body was placed on this couch, and I was only ten years old. They had this solu tion in a china bowl and I had to keep his face moistened all the time. It was like wet compresses on his face to keep it from turning dark. So that's what I had to do as a youngster.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Did it upset you?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: No, I just had to do ... I was asked to do it and it was my Marie Flodberg iO responsibility and I don't know that I was upset about it.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Can you describe anymore of what happened when he died? Your mother's and father's reaction?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: No, other than I was in school that day and I had been home for lunch. I was standing at the back window in the schoolroom and I could see our house from that window and something told me that I had to go home. It was the Saturday before Easter Sunday and I just felt that I had to go home something was wrong and I had to be there. When I got there, he had just passed away. I had to call the doctor by phone and say that the youngster had passed away.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Did they light candles around him or anything like that?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Mostly Catholics did those things I think. No, we didn't have any of those rituals.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Was he buried in your home?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: He was buried at the cemetery there at Traer.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Did the friends and relatives come?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: All the neighborhood. No, all the relatives were out of state; they were in Iowa and they wouldn't come to a youngster's Marie Flodberg 11 funeral. But the neighbors and the friends. I don't remember any of the church service. I don't remember that at all. I think probably the youngsters stayed at home instead of going to the service. But I do remember when my grandfather died. That was before we moved to Idaho and I was about three and a half years old. My mother had breakfast ready and she said, "Go up stairs and see why Grandpa doesn't come down for breakfast." So I went upstairs to see and he was lying on the bed; he had his underwear on and one sock on and he had fallen across the bed. So, I came downstairs and remember standing in the doorway of the stairway telling my mother that Grandpa wouldn't talk to me. I don't remember any of the things that happened during the funeral until they had brought the casket into the house. They brought the casket into the parlor and it was a big beautiful black shiny thing with silver handles. My dad raised me up and lifted me up so that I could see Grandpa. He had the most beautiful hair; he had a wave across the top, it was silver white. So I do remember. Of course, we had a picture of him, too. That probably impressed a little more firmly on my mind.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: How old were you then?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: This was the summer before I was four years old.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: That was longer ago than the other one and you remembered it.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I remember when my grandfather was alive. That was when I Marie Flodberg 12 was only three years old, that summer, a little more than three years old. I can remember him carrying me around the yard so I didn't have to walk.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: He pampered you.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: He was just real good to me.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: It's nice to have a grandparent who will pamper you.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I don't remember my grandmother because she died when I was only about a year old, so I don't remember that. But I do remem ber Grandpa. He used to go for a walk and take me with him. He had a neighbor boy that had a goat and he had a wagon that he hitched this goat to and often times he'd come over and put me in that wagon, it was about five feet long. I don't know whether you've seen those wagons they hitched goats to.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: No, I don't think I have.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: They are about that long and yay wide. He'd come over to the house, they lived across the road, our neighbor farmer and he was probably about ten or 12, maybe 14 years old. Take me for a ride and ride up and down the road with a goat hitched to it. They kept that goat in the pig hard; they smelled too much to keep them elsewhere, so he was in the hogs' yard. Marie Flodberg 13

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Do goats and pigs get along?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Oh yeah; I suppose if maybe the pigs got in the way the goat would thump them or shove them out of the way. I don't remember that, but I do remember seeing him feed him at the trough with the pigs. That was about the same summer that my grandfather died.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: I'd like to know your husband's name?

speaker: MR
words: Herman L. Flodberg.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: When was he born?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: That was in 1895.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: And where was he born?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Troy, Idaho.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: What year were you married?

speaker: Connie Richards
words: So, he was pretty old when you got married; and you were too.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Yes, I was 40 years old. Marie Flodberg 14

speaker: Connie Richards
words: What did you do all that time before you got married?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, I went to grade school for four years. Then, we went back to Iowa and I went through the seventh grade in Iowa, and that's when I lived with this friend, and she wanted to come to Payette to visit her relatives. I said, "All right, I'll go with you." So I told my folks I was on my way to Idaho. Well, then I came to Idaho and I went to Boise and first I went to business college for a year and I worked with the Pioneer Tent and Awning Company. Then I decided I'd better go to high school. So I started in a high school. Then, while I was in high school and before I finished, I went into nurses' training. I went to business college in Boise and from there I went to Spokane and I took my nurses' training in Spokane. Then I worked in a hospital. I was in charge of a hospital in Hailey, Idaho. I saw some of these abortions that they are talking about now and nothing was said about it. The patients came in and wanted to be rid of the babies and the doctor performed the operation; I gave the anes thetic.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Did you realize what was happening?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Sure I did. I didn't say anything and he didn't say anything.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Did you think that the woman had a right to do that?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Sure they do. Some of them were girls that were not married. Marie Flodberg 15 One of them was a girl who was going to be married in the Mormon Temple. She came and he did a Cesarean abortion on her instead of the normal way that they do it usually.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Why did he do that?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, she was a little farther along than she should've been. I think she was three months or four months, something like that. So, there you are. Her sister was watching the operation and she got faint and went out just before the doctor made the incision. Oh, I could tell a lot of things about the doctors, but, of course, you don't dare. So don't mention that.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Where were you married?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: In Moscow.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: At a church there?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: At the Norwegian Parsonage.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: When did your husband die?

speaker: Connie Richards
words: What year were you married then, again?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: In 1934. Marie Flodberg 16

speaker: Connie Richards
words: You were married in '34 and he died in '38? You were only married for four years?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Four years and one month.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: What was your husband's occupation?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: He was for the PFI. He worked under the state forester before he went over to PFI. He continued practically in the same line of work -- woodsman.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: He liked being in the woods?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Yes.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Did you have children, then?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: No.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Now, you already told me your education. Let's see if I can remember. You went through eighth grade and had high school?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: But I didn't complete high school, no. When it came to regis tering for nursing, they accepted my business college credits and the combination of the business college credits and what high school credits I had was equivalent of a high school education. Marie Flodberg 17

speaker: Connie Richards
words: And how long was your training for nursing?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Three years.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Did you have a degree when you were finished? A bachelors?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: No, I didn't have a bachelor's degree. They didn't give bachelor's degree for that. Just a registered nurse.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Now, I imagine you've had quite a few jobs in your life.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, no, not too many, no.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Can you tell me which ones?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: As I say, I worked in Hailey from out of training and I was there for a year. I had charge of a small hospital, a private hospital, really. I gave the anesthetics for all these surgeries, one kind or another, and took care of the patients and cooked for them.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: You did everything?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Yes. Well, we only had about five patients and so there wasn't too much to do. It was to your convenience. You can if you want to. Marie Flodberg 18

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Did you like that kind of nursing?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, it's all right, it's a job. If you want to work, it's all right.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: What did you do after that?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Then I went back to Iowa for a time to see my folks, I guess for a month or six weeks. The doctor from Pocatello wired me wanting to know if I would accept a job in the office. So I was there for seven years in Pocatello. I was an office nurse and I gave anesthetics for all the minor surgery.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: And after that, did you have another job?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: After that, I got married.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: When you got married, did you stay at home or did you work?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: No, I stayed at home most of the time. I worked part of the time; I worked at the hospital in Moscow at that time . We were living in Troy. Tray was Vollmer at that time. There was a Post Office and as years gone by it was a freight and stock. So, on the old maps of Idaho it's listed as Vollmer. It's 16 miles out of Moscow, so I would drive back and forth. After my husband died, I went East and bought a car and drove a car back. Marie Flodberg 19

speaker: Connie Richards
words: What year was that?

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Was that your first car?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: No, I bought a car in 1923, something like that. Had a Ford.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: How did your husband die?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, to tell you the honest truth, I don't know. Too much drink, mostly. But I think he had something else wrong because he wasn't sick too long. It just happened very suddenly. It was best.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: How old were you then?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I was 42 or 43, I guess.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Was that pretty much of a shock to you?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: No. It was just one of those things. When you have some thing like that in a home, it's a relief. You just put up with drinking so long. He was his own worst enemy and so I felt he was released. I would have left if he would've live much longer.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: You must have been pretty independent by the time you got Marie Flodberg 20 married. You were sure of what you wanted to do.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, I had a car. I came to Lewiston to take charge of a small hospital and when I got there and met the doctor, oh, I met the doctor and he had an empty house that he was going to equip at the nursing home and when I moved there he had two beds. He had, a couple of days after I came, he had one patient. He had one of these old type desks and on the right hand bottom drawer was filled full of sawdust and he spat into that -- he chewed tobacco. So that got to me. I thought, "Well, of all the filthy things, and to think he was going to operate and things like that." So, I only stayed there for a few months, then I went to Orofino and I worked at the hospital there for a while. Well, that's where I met Herman was at Orofino.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: How did you meet him?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, he was hospitalized as a patient and I was working at the hospital.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Do you have interests and hobbies that you can tell me about?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, what can you do when you can't see?

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Is it cataracts?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: No, it's deterioration of the retina. There's nothing that Marie Flodberg 21 can be done for it. I will gradually lose my sight probably. Maybe not all of it, but it's getting darker and nothing can be done. So, what are you going to do?

speaker: Connie Richards
words: I have very, very poor vision without glasses. I have contacs right now.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: You are probably nearsighted, then.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Yes, I am nearsighted.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: When I was working in Pocatello with this doctor, I learned all those things and I can just about diagnose you. It was inter esting work and we had quite a number of interesting patients. Never anything like I have; we had cataracts, sure, but I don't ever remember a doctor diagnose a blindness like I have. Of course, people are living to be older and they do things. We had older patients; we had patients that were 80 years old, but I don't think nothing like that ever came about.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Does that make you angry that that's happening to you? I mean, because you seem like you are so active in every way.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Why should you? It doesn't do any good. No, it's just something that you have to put up with and hope that you don't go completely blind. Marie Flodberg 22

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Then you accept it?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, you have to. There's no two ways about it. You know, I've seen several doctors and there's nothing to be done.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Well, before that happened to your eyes, did you have hobbies that you liked?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: When I had an acre of hillside where my home was, I land scaped that. That was just a side line; I did that when I wasn't working. But I worked at the hospital and drove back and forth to Moscow, so most of the time I was working in Moscow in surgery or on the floors or wherever they needed me. One year I was in the diet kitchen and in charge of diets.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Do you enjoy cooking and baking and things like that?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Yes. I could serve a better meal than the dietician.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Do you belong to Connie's group? What is she in charge of?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: To tell you the truth, I don't know what the name of her group is. I go to some of these things. I belong to a health group. We have a health group connected with the County Health Association and different groups that are here. They call them the Silver Seniors. They're just local groups, there's probably 15 or 20 women here, there are about five groups here in the center Marie Flodberg 23 that meet at different times. Instead of getting too large, we have some that belong to one group and others belong to another group. But they all do about the same thing. Nothing much, maybe I shouldn't say that, but they collect some money and they go on trips and sometimes, folks feel bad because they couldn't go on the trip. This money business is a mistake, I think, because there's usually feelings about it, sometimes hard feelings. You can't participate for certain reasons and that was on a date and you couldn't go.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Have you ever won an award, honor, or ribbon for anything?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, when I was at Moscow for six years I was in charge of the women's division at the fair, and I always had blue ribbons on cooking and sewing. I did a lot of sewing, a lot of sewing. Blue ribbons in sewing and baking and cooking and what not. I wond an electric roaster one year, a drawing in Troy, the first year I was there. Another year I took a chance on a white faced steer and won a 750 pound steer. I took it to Spokane to the stock yard and I got $220 for it, so my dollar was well invested. So I've been lucky in drawing some things of that sort quite often.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Now, do you think of yourself more as a rural woman rather than a city girl? Marie Flodberg 24

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I don't know.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Have you lived your life in rural areas?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Mostly. In Troy, I lived 16 miles outside of Moscow. I drove back and forth to work and that was from '34 on until I came here four years ago, or five years ago. I've been here just five years.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Were you living on a farm there?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I had rock gardens, rock walls, and planted flowers and shrubs and things. It was 225 feet frontage and that was rock garden, rock wall, flowers and shrubs. I should have pictures of people, I think I do somewhere around.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Can you tell me about your family life when you were married?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, he was in the woods and I was there and that's all.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: You weren't together too much?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: No. He came home maybe once every two weeks or once a month. He was usually up in the woods 50 or 60 miles away from home. Sometimes it was convenient for him to come home. He was camp clerk part of the time and so he had to stay. Marie Flodberg 25

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Can you describe some of the things that you and your sisters did when you were young?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I can't remember much of anything there.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Like you were telling me about the goats and the wagon.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I was the oldest child then, and my sister was a baby at that time, so I was the first one. I don't remember her, other than she was the baby. The other one, she's just a year and a half younger than I am. My other sister was two years younger than that so they were too small for me to play with or think about.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Maybe you could think about a special Christmas or a holiday or something. Can you remember what your mom or dad did for Christmas? Did you have a Christmas tree?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I don't remember any Christmases at all until we went to Idaho.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: And what happened there?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I don't remember anything except one Halloween evening, one of the neighbor girls came over and said that we'd better be careful because the neighbor boys would probably come over and do all sorts of damage. I was about eight years old about that Marie Flodberg 26 time and I thought, "All right, I'll fix it." We had a picket fence and I stretched a rope across the gate about six inches above the ground. I waited till it got dark so that nobody would see me do it, and if they opened the gate they'd come in and fall. And the neighbor girls did it -- they were the ones.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: So it got the girls instead of the boys?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I did the same thing out at the barn, but the boys didn't show up. I did the same thing out at the barn at the gate next to the barn. I got a rope and stretched it in case anybody come and let the gate down and tried to cross the fence, they'd get caught. So, I had ideas then, I was up to mischief. I could always climb a tree a lot higher than any of the boys.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: When you met your husband, did you court at all?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, when you meet a patient and the fellow is down in bed, you don't do much.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Did you get married soon after he was released from the hospital?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: We married in March. I met him early in December, so it wasn't very long.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Can you tell me what were the reasons that you got married? Marie Flodberg 27

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, why does anybody get married?

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Well, some people have different reasons.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I don't know.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: You were just in love?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, I guess he just felt he wanted a home. We were married and went to Spokane and bought our furniture and this is what we bought.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: What did you used to do for recreation and relaxation for yourself? Did you ever go places with girlfriends?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: When you live alone, you don't go anyplace. When you are working at the hospital, driving back and forth, you are busy everyday, you don't go places very often. You don't go to dances when you are alone. If you don't have a dancing partner, why, you don't go. I like to dance.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: When you were married did you husband like to dance?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Yes.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: So, you did some dancing then? Marie Flodberg 28

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Not very much because he was working and I was working. No, we didn't go to dances very much. A few times, but not much.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Most of the women I have talked to get married much younger and I'd kind of like to know why you didn't get married younger.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: As me another foolish question! To young to tend with.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: So you were an exception then, because most women got married young then.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, I tell you, before I went to Boise we used to go to dances. One of the boys there I would dance with. There was never thoughts when we were together. There was never any demonstration of affections or anything.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: You were pretty strong minded. You wanted to be a nurse and you were going to go ahead and do that?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Yeah.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: One of these questions here talks about supporting your family. I guess you have pretty much financially supported yourself most of your life.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Yes. Marie Flodberg 29

speaker: Connie Richards
words: When you were married, you continued to work?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Sure. Not all the time, but she spent part of his money for parties for the other men. He said they had to share the expense for the parties, so there were times when $100 would go for pay- ment of a party for somebody else. I said, "Why?" He said you had to in order to be a good sport. I said that I would be a bad sport if I had to do that. There was no sense in that, paying for the party for the boss, or paying for the boss's party, I should say. Let him pay his own. No, I always had my own money and spent it, saved it and what not.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: I want you to tell me some more about the things you are doing right now. What did Connie say that you do? You take mail for somebody?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I go get the keys for the people here. I stop and pick up their key and then get their mail and bring it to them. Some of those people who are not able to be out.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Do you take it right to their door?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Yes. I go in and pick up their key and get the mail and usually I come home with something to eat for lunch or supper.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Somebody gives you something? Marie Flodberg 30

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Always get something. Today, I got a big bowl of noodles and turkey and lettuce salad and I was asked at another place for a beef hamburger and french fries, so I had the beef ham burger and french fries, so I'll have the noodles another time.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Isn't that something? It seems like a nice little community here for you.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Oh, yes.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: You have people to visit with and people to ...

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, it breaks the monotony for those who don't get out. But, they have other friends that come in. I spend about two hours every morning gathering keys and waiting for the mail and tqking the mail back and posting their letters.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: And everybody kind of helps everybody else, huh? Like, you bring the mail and they give you some food.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: If you were talking to some younger girls today, what su~ges tions would you want to make to them? What things would you talk to them about?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I think that's pretty much up to the individual. It's hard to tell someone else what to do and what not to do. You know that, too. You have certain ideas about what you would like to Marie Flodberg 31 do. Things you hear about some of these people and you think, well, maybe you could help them by telling them to do this, and so they don't want to be told.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Well, if a young girl came to you and said, "Bunny, I want you to share some advice with me and tell me what to watch out for in the future and tell me, from all your experience of living." You must have some idea about ...

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Things are not what they were 50 years ago when I was young, when I came out of training.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: It might have even been harder for a girl like you to be like she was.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Not for anyone who was independent and thinks she knows it all. I would hesitate to talk to anyone. Of course, there are a few things you probably might advise them about. But, not having had any girls, it's hard to tell. You almost have to live with a youngster in order to know what to suggest. There are things, everyone likes different things. We don't all like to do the same thing.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Did you decide that you didn't want to have children?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: No, it's just one of those things. When you are 40 years old, you really don't expect those things. Marie Flodberg 32

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Do you get any magazines or newspapers? Or would it be impossible for you to read them?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I get all my books and magazines from "Sing Song Records." They are furnished by the Library of the Blind and we get maga zines. I get the Reader's Digest, Harper's, and National Geographic.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Do you get recent issues on records?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: They come every month. The Reader's Digest comes regularly, the first of every month, and it's the full magazine from begin ning to end: table of contents, the funny little quips at the foot of the page, and all the rest of it. Harper's is a very interesting, more so than well, you know what the Reader's Digest is. Harper's is something that a lot of adults subscribe to. There are a lot of interesting articles in Harper's.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Yeah, we get Harper's at our house.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: And then, National Geographic. Now I am reading Celia Garth. It's a story during the Revolutionary days. The other one that I've just finished was Calico Palace, about a young girl who comes amiss because she had no home, or her mother didn't want her, really. She came to California with the first gold rush trip that left San Francisco and went up into the mountains. Marie Flodberg 33 A young man that she married, he had a wife; but, they were married and after six months they separated again. They decided that that was the thing to do and then, later one she married again and had a child. Her child and husband died within a week of one another. Later on in the book she married another man and suppose she was kind of happy. There were a lot of trials and tribulations all through her story.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: How long does it take you to listen to a story like that?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: It depends on how many records there are. There were 19 records in this Calico Palace, and I didn't listen to this Celia Garth. That's a story of Revolutionary times. There were quite a bit of records there, too, I think probably about 12 or 13. But the Reader's Digest comes in four records. National Geo graphic comes in two. Harper's is on four records.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Then do you return those?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I can keep Harper's; they don't ask them to be returned. The Reader's Digest, the National Geographic, and the others, they're furnished from the Library for the Blind out of Boise. Those are all free, they come to us post free and we take them over to the post office and the mail carrier picks them up and returns them. They're all free to us. We should pay for them by right and I intend to give the library something for it. Marie Flodberg 34

speaker: Connie Richards
words: That sounds like a good service for you.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, it gives you something, it gives you some worthwhile information. You can get instructions in typing. I had an instruction record on typing and I sent it back. I should've kept it, so I'm going to send for it again and bring my typing up to date.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: When you came out here, you ran away?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, I didn't run away. This girl was coming to visit, her cousin's in Idaho and I happened to have an uncle there, so I thought, "Well, I'll go with you." I was only 16 or 17 at the time, I guess. I had worked and earned some money and had enough money to pay my railroad fare, so I came West. Of course, we had lived at Payette, so I knew people there and my uncle lived there, so I wasn't coming in among strangers.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Did your family know you were coming, then, or not?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, we had written to her cousin and her aunt and uncle and told them that we were coming, and I wrote to my uncle and told him.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: And how did you come out?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: By train. Then it was ten years before I went home again. Marie Flodberg 35

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Was your family mad at you?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: No. They knew me.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: They expected you by then?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I was too independent.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: I must say that it was exceptional that you were that way. In those days, women weren't supposed to be that way.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: When I was 14, a neighbor called and wanted to know if I'd do some sewing for her and I sure, "Sure." So I went out to her home; she had twins and a girl who was two years older. The twins were five and the girl was seven. So, I was there for three weeks and sewed for her, dresses and panties and things of that sort that youngsters wore. Fifty cents a day. When I finished there, another lady called and wanted to know if I would do some sewing for her and I said, "Sure." So she said, "Oh, I' 11 pay you 7 5 cents a day." By that time I was in seventh heaven. So I was there for two or three weeks and I remember one of the things that I made for her was a purple vellard [?] dress. Beautiful material. And you [unintelligible] material like that and it is really beautiful. We made a yolk on the dress and it was embroidered net. So, instead of leaving it plain, I took the purple thread and button holder on around the design and that just set off the dress. Marie Flodberg 36

speaker: Connie Richards
words: I don't know what kind of material that is.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: It's an older material; they don't have it anymore. It's a felt material, so it was soft and it had a print in it, a floral design, not very heavy, just l~ghtly designed. It was a dainty design, I should say.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: She trusted you quite a bit.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Well, I made some other dresses first and then she had me do that.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: She brought out that first before she had you use the more expensive material. What other materials did they use then?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I think the materials were a bit more cottons and things of that sort. A lot of pretty cottons. I don't remember anything other than those vellards [?]. Those vellards were a nice dressy silk, they had a soft feeling. I don't know of anything we have today that is like that at all.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Do you have pictures when you were younger?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I had my nurses' pictures and that's all.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Where are they, do you know? Marie Flodberg 37

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I have a Kodak album somewhere, but I couldn't tell you where.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Because one of the things that we can do as part of our project is if someone has an old picture, we can promise to be very careful and borrow it and the photographer can blow it up and make a new picture for our files.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I'll go through some things and I'll see if I can find one, but I didn't have many pictures. I don't make a pretty picture.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: I don't believe that! You did something different than most women did at that time. Did you feel like other women were angry with you or how did they treat you? You know, women who did more traditional things at that time.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I don't know that I even considered that. It never bothered me. I did as I pleased and let them do as they pleased. If they didn't like it. I was more or less independent, I think. They may have envied.me, but it didn't bother me if they did.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: You've spent a lot of years nursing then, more than anything else?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: And in between, I did dress making. When I wasn't working at the hospital and had spare time and was with friends, I Marie Flodberg 38 usually sewed. I usually sewed when I was with friends, if they had sewing to do, why, I was there. I had a friend in Sandpoint and stayed with her at times and she says, "Oh, I have some material and I like it when you make a dress for me, it always looks different." And I made one dress for her and we didn't put any trimming on it, but we bought some buttons. So, we went to Spokane and stopped at the Crescent. I don't know whether you know Spokane or not.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Just a little.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: It's one of the big department stores. Of course, that was 20 or 30 years ago, too. And she asked to see some buttons, and then after she had seen what was in the case there, she says, "Is this all the buttons you have?" And the clerk says, "Well, we have some more expensive buttons." So she says, "May I see them, please?" She got out some of the most expensive buttons and she picked out three of them and they were $1.25 a piece! That was all the trimming that was on the dress and it set off the dress.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Sometimes they are prettier like that. I've done some sewing too and I don't usually put too many fancy things on it, but I like nice buttons. Did you make the dress that you have on?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: No. Marie Flodberg 39

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Do you have anything left that you've made for yourself?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Oh, I have a few things, yes.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Would you mind showing them to me?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: No. I've got the dress that I had one; that was the dress I changed after I heard you were coming. I thought maybe I'd better put on something else. When I was with the fiddlers group in Moscow, and I belonged to the square dance then, so I square danced. When I was ready to come to Lewiston, one of the women there had gained 15 pounds in weight and she had dresses that she couldn't wear and never would wear again. So I fell heir to ten dresses and this happens to be one of them. They all fit and then when I came here, there was one of the folks that lived here who had lost 12 pounds and she had dresses that were just my size. So I got five dresses from here. Since I've been here, I haven't bought a thing.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: That's good because clothing is really high right now.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Yes.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: If I had more time I would do more sewing.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: I like to sew, I always did. Marie Flodberg 40

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Yeah, I do enjoy sewing, too. I just don't seem to have the time lately.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: The thing is that some of these dresses that I have now are for short sleeve, and with all these blotches that have appeared on my arms, I look better with long sleeves than I do in short sleeves.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: Those aren't blotches, those are senior citizens' freckles.

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Senior freckles, I agree. Probably now that I can't see too well I can't see them, but those that are real dark do show up a bit.

speaker: Connie Richards
words: It looks like those are some of your nursing shoes that you have on. Did you used to wear those shoes when you were nursing?

speaker: Marie Flodberg
words: Yes. Well, these are new ones. They probably need cleaning.
